payload.summary: Medieval Mon kingdom in lower Burma (modern Myanmar). Its kings styled themselves 'Lord of the White Elephants,' white elephants being sacred symbols of royal power in Southeast Asia.
Formal regnal title of Burmese and Mon monarchs; possession of a white (albino) elephant was considered divine sanction for a ruler's legitimacy.
Thailand's Chakri dynasty monarchs. The white elephant appeared on the Siamese royal flag until 1917, reflecting the same Southeast Asian tradition of sacred albino elephants.
The House of Hanover ruled Britain 1714–1901. Their heraldic white horse (the 'White Horse of Hanover') appeared on the Hanoverian standard and English county emblems.
The Habsburg emperors claimed succession from the Roman Caesars; white was the Austrian imperial military color, seen on uniforms and the imperial standard.

annotations.surface: a white stone marked a joyful day

payload.summary: Roman custom of marking lucky days with a white chalk stone (calculus albus) on the calendar, contrasted with black stones for unlucky days. Referenced by Pliny and others.
Period ethnonym for Native Americans. Melville refers specifically to the wampum belt tradition among northeastern tribes, where white shell beads signified peace and solemn pledges.
Wampum belts of white shell beads (from whelk) carried diplomatic and ceremonial weight among Iroquois and Algonquian peoples; white signified peace, purple/black signified war or mourning.
Zoroastrians, whose sacred fire altars were central to worship. The white or purest flame was considered the holiest manifestation of Ahura Mazda's divine light.

annotations.surface: Great Jove himself being made incarnate in a snow-white bull

payload.summary: Refers to the myth of Europa: Zeus transformed into a white bull to abduct her. Also echoes the white bulls sacrificed to Jupiter in Roman triumphal rites.

annotations.surface: midwinter sacrifice of the sacred White Dog

payload.summary: The Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) White Dog Feast, held at midwinter, involved sacrificing a ritually strangled white dog as a pure messenger to the Creator (Great Spirit).
From Latin alba, 'white.' The alb is the long white liturgical vestment worn by Christian clergy; Melville correctly traces the name to the Latin root for whiteness.
The Book of Revelation. White robes given to martyrs (Rev. 6:11), the twenty-four elders in white (Rev. 4:4), and the great white throne judgment (Rev. 20:11) are all cited here.
The polar bear (Ursus maritimus) was a fixture of 19th-century sublime natural history, frequently cited as the most formidable Arctic predator and a symbol of terrifying otherness.
Refers to the tiger's striped patterning as if it were a coat of arms; 'heraldic' evokes formal, decorative display, contrasting with the shark's and bear's plain, unmarked whiteness.
Opening words of the Roman Catholic Mass for the Dead: 'Requiem aeternam dona eis' ('Grant them eternal rest'). Melville derives the French word 'requin' (shark) from this liturgical term.

French word for shark. Melville's folk etymology linking it to 'Requiem' is fanciful; the actual etymology is disputed. The connection nonetheless serves his thematic argument about whiteness and death.

Anticipates the footnote reference to Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), in which the killing of an albatross brings a curse. Melville credits not Coleridge but Nature as the original source of the bird's dread.

annotations.surface: Not Coleridge first threw that spell

payload.summary: Melville deliberately subordinates literary tradition to natural fact, arguing the albatross's terror precedes and exceeds any poet's rendering of it — a claim about the limits of art versus the sublime.
Horizontal covers over the ship's main cargo openings, flush with the deck — a flat surface where a large seabird could be pinned down by wind or crew.
The Ark of the Covenant, carried by the Israelites; its transport was attended by divine presence and strict ritual. The albatross's spread wings recall the cherubim atop the Ark.
Genesis 18: Abraham prostrates himself before three divine visitors at Mamre. Ishmael's involuntary bow mirrors that reverent submission before the numinous.
Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798), in which a sailor kills an albatross and suffers supernatural punishment. Melville insists his awe preceded any literary influence.
Sailors' dialectal name for the albatross, probably from a word meaning 'simpleton' (the bird's tameness made it easy to catch). Unknown outside maritime use.
'Solecism' normally means a grammatical or social blunder; here Melville uses it to mean a contradiction in terms — calling a bird 'grey albatross' when whiteness is the albatross's defining quality.
A practice of attaching a leather tag inscribed with the ship's name, date, and position to a captured seabird before releasing it, as a primitive message-in-a-bottle for tracking voyages.

annotations.surface: wing-folding, the invoking, and adoring cherubim

payload.summary: Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1 describe cherubim with multiple wings, some folded, surrounding God's throne in ceaseless adoration — the released albatross joins this celestial company.
A legendary wild white stallion reported by 19th-century travelers on the Great Plains; figures in Washington Irving and Josiah Gregg's accounts, becoming a symbol of untameable frontier freedom.
Xerxes I, Persian king who led an enormous army into Greece (480 BCE). Melville uses him as a type of supreme sovereign commanding vast hosts.

annotations.surface: that chosen star which every evening leads on the hosts of light

payload.summary: The evening star (Venus/Hesperus), which appears to lead the stars across the sky. The image echoes Milton's description of the morning star in Paradise Lost.
Melville frames the American West as a prelapsarian Eden, contrasting it with the corrupted Old World — a common Romantic trope that the White Steed embodies as an Adamic, sinless creature.
The Ohio River, notable for its broad, steady, seemingly endless flow — used here as a simile for the unbroken stream of horse herds across the plains.
A sudden, violent storm in tropical or subtropical seas, named for the white foam and spray that mark its approach rather than the dark clouds typical of other squalls.

Jean Froissart (c.1337–1405), Franco-Flemish chronicler whose *Chronicles* record the Hundred Years' War era. Melville refers to his account of the White Hoods (Chaperons Blancs) of Ghent, a 14th-century Flemish rebel faction.
The Chaperons Blancs, a guild-based rebel movement in Ghent (1379–82) who wore white hoods as their emblem and violently resisted Flemish aristocratic authority.
Phrase from Job 18:14 (KJV), where death is called 'the king of terrors.' Melville links it to the pale rider of Revelation 6:8.
Revelation 6:8: 'And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death.' The Greek *chloros* (pale/ashen) underlies 'pallid' here.
Christian feast fifty days after Easter (Pentecost). In England it was a major holiday with processions, but Melville stresses its eerie, wintry associations rather than its festive ones.
Carmelite friar, so called from the white mantle worn over the brown habit. 'White Nun' similarly refers to certain orders such as the Cistercian or Premonstratensian nuns.
The central keep of the Tower of London, built by William the Conqueror c. 1078. Its pale Caen stone and history of royal imprisonment and execution give it its sinister reputation.
The main outer-gate tower of the Tower of London complex, through which condemned prisoners entered. Less famous than the White Tower but equally storied.
Northeastern U.S. mountain range; its highest peak, Mt. Washington, is notorious for sudden violent weather and was already a site of sublime, death-tinged tourism in Melville's era.
Arctic inlet of northern Russia, ice-bound much of the year. Its name and remoteness gave it an aura of desolation for nineteenth-century readers.
The Harz mountains of central Germany were the legendary haunt of witches and spirits; the Blocksberg (Brocken) was their traditional sabbath-ground, familiar from Goethe's Faust and German folklore.
The Brocken, highest peak of the Harz, site of the Walpurgisnacht witches' sabbath in German legend and in Goethe's Faust, Part I.
Francisco Pizarro, Spanish conquistador who conquered the Inca Empire and founded Lima in 1535. Melville uses him as a marker of Lima's antiquity and violent colonial origins.

annotations.surface: lead assures him he is still off soundings

payload.summary: A lead (sounding lead) is a weighted line dropped to measure sea depth. 'Off soundings' means the water is too deep to reach bottom — i.e., no hidden rocks below.
A howdah is the canopied seat mounted on an elephant's back. Melville uses it metaphorically: the Andes wear their snow-caps like a howdah atop a great beast.
Literally 'light of hand' (French); sleight-of-hand conjuring. Melville applies it to the uncanny optical illusions produced by Antarctic ice and atmosphere.
'Hypo' is short for hypochondria, used in the period to mean melancholy or morbid depression — the same affliction Ishmael cites in Chapter 1 as driving him to sea.
Tanned bison hide used as a blanket or cloak; widely traded on the American frontier. Its raw animal smell would be wholly alien to a Vermont-raised horse.
Mid-19th-century Americans used 'Oregon' loosely for the vast trans-Mississippi West. Bison herds had not roamed New England for generations, making the colt's fear instinctive rather than learned.
'Windrowed' means gathered into long parallel ridges by wind, as hay is raked into rows. Transfers an agricultural term to drifted snow on open prairie.

annotations.surface: invisible spheres were formed in fright

payload.summary: Echoes Gnostic and Calvinist cosmologies in which a fallen or malevolent demiurge shaped the hidden structure of creation, contrasting with the benevolent surface of the visible world.
Alludes to Exodus 33–34, where Moses veils his face after seeing God, and to the Temple veil torn at the Crucifixion (Matthew 27:51); whiteness simultaneously reveals and conceals the divine.

Melville anticipates the physics of white light: white is not a pigment colour but the presence of all wavelengths, while the absence of all light is black. The paradox—absence yet totality—drives the chapter's argument.

Period term for scientists/physicists, here invoking Newtonian optics: light appears colourless but contains all colours, revealed by a prism. Melville uses this to argue nature's colours are illusions laid over a white void.

Echoes Proverbs and the Whore of Babylon (Revelation 17), the painted woman whose beauty conceals corruption. Nature as cosmetically adorned deceiver is a Calvinist trope Melville intensifies to cosmic scale.

Recalls Shakespeare's Juliet refusing to enter 'a charnel-house' (Romeo and Juliet III.ii); more broadly, the charnel-house as a repository of bones underlies the harlot metaphor: beauty masking death.

Arctic travellers wore tinted snow-goggles to prevent snow-blindness. Melville uses this as a figure for those who strip away nature's coloured illusions and face the blank white truth directly, at cost of their sight.
Leprosy in the Bible (Leviticus 13) manifests as white patches; the leper is unclean and cast out. A universe revealed as white is thus figured as diseased, cursed, and untouchable.
